blocks.text: 1. Adadelta
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444932861-787919528.png

Adagrad's ever-shrinking learning rate problem, the previous topic's genuine, real weakness, needed a direct, targeted fix. Adadelta makes one deliberate, targeted change specifically to fix this exact issue.

It keeps Adagrad's genuine per-weight adaptation strength, already covered fully in the previous topic, while removing its specific, well-documented flaw, a direct, focused evolution rather than an entirely separate, unrelated algorithm.
2. A Sliding Window Instead of Unlimited Accumulation

blocks.alt: A Sliding Window Instead of Unlimited Accumulation
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444932861-853172493.png

This connects back to Adagrad's own ever-growing accumulated sum, already covered in its own dedicated topic. Adadelta uses a sliding, decaying window of recent squared gradients instead, rather than accumulating every single gradient since training began.

Old, distant updates gradually fade out of this window over time, rather than accumulating forever the way they genuinely did under Adagrad, directly addressing the exact source of that earlier algorithm's own weakness.
3. The Decay Factor
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444932861-987090580.png

A genuinely important parameter is the decay rate, controlling exactly how quickly older squared gradients actually fade out of Adadelta's sliding window. Recent squared gradients get weighted more heavily under this scheme.

Older squared gradients get weighted progressively less, and gradually fade out entirely as training continues, exactly the mechanism that gives this sliding window its own genuinely bounded, well-behaved size, rather than growing without any limit at all.

blocks.text: 4. Fixing the Shrinkage Problem
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933096-94534903.png

This connects back to Adagrad's ever-shrinking rate, already covered in genuine depth in the previous topic. Since old updates genuinely fade out of Adadelta's window, the accumulated sum stays bounded, rather than growing without any limit forever.

This means learning rates stay genuinely usable throughout the entire training run, even a very long one, directly solving the exact stalling problem already covered as Adagrad's own genuine, real weakness.
5. No Explicit Learning Rate Needed
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933096-921307571.png

A genuinely distinctive property, worth understanding clearly, is that Adadelta was originally designed to need no manually chosen learning rate at all, a genuinely unusual property compared to essentially every other optimizer covered throughout this module.

It derives an appropriate update scale directly from the accumulated gradient and update history itself, a self-contained, self-scaling mechanism that, in its original design, removed one entire hyperparameter a practitioner would otherwise need to choose and tune.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This learning-rate-free design was a genuinely notable, distinctive feature of Adadelta's original formulation, removing an entire hyperparameter that essentially every other optimizer covered throughout this module still requires choosing.

blocks.text: 6. How Real Implementations Actually Handle This

This connects back to hyperparameters, a concept already established throughout this course. Real, practical implementations often still include a learning rate parameter anyway, despite Adadelta's original, learning-rate-free design already covered in the previous section.

This provides an extra, optional degree of control, even though the original design did not strictly require it, a genuinely pragmatic compromise between Adadelta's elegant original theory and the practical flexibility real-world training often genuinely benefits from.
7. A Direct Comparison to Adagrad
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933096-592294382.png

A direct comparison is worth stating clearly. Adagrad accumulates an ever-growing sum, already covered in genuine depth in its own topic, eventually stalling training, genuinely problematic specifically for long training runs.

Adadelta instead maintains a bounded, sliding-window sum, staying genuinely usable indefinitely, directly solving that exact problem while preserving the core per-weight adaptation idea both algorithms genuinely share.

blocks.text: 8. The RMSProp Connection
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933096-148570222.png

This connects forward to RMSProp, the very next topic in this module. RMSProp was developed around the same time as Adadelta, addressing this exact same ever-shrinking problem already covered throughout this topic.

It uses a genuinely similar sliding-window idea, through a somewhat different, independently-derived formula, a genuinely interesting case of two separate research efforts converging on a closely related solution to the exact same real, practical problem.
9. Recognizing When Adadelta Is Genuinely Worth Choosing

Long training runs, where Adagrad's own weakness, already covered throughout this topic, genuinely becomes a real problem, are a direct case for Adadelta, its bounded window directly solving this exact issue.

A genuine preference for fewer hyperparameters to actually tune also fits Adadelta well, since its original, learning-rate-free design can genuinely simplify setup, even though real implementations often still offer that parameter as an optional extra, already covered earlier in this topic.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly compares Adagrad and Adadelta's accumulated sums over many training steps, illustrating the bounded-versus-unbounded behavior covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def adagrad_accumulate(accumulated, gradient):
    return accumulated + gradient ** 2

def adadelta_accumulate(accumulated, gradient, decay=0.9):
    return decay * accumulated + (1 - decay) * gradient ** 2

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
gradients = rng.normal(loc=0.3, scale=0.1, size=200)  # 200 simulated training steps

adagrad_sum = 0.0
adadelta_sum = 0.0
adagrad_history = []
adadelta_history = []

for gradient in gradients:
    adagrad_sum = adagrad_accumulate(adagrad_sum, gradient)
    adadelta_sum = adadelta_accumulate(adadelta_sum, gradient)
    adagrad_history.append(adagrad_sum)
    adadelta_history.append(adadelta_sum)

print(f"After 200 steps:")
print(f"  Adagrad's accumulated sum: {adagrad_history[-1]:.4f} (kept growing throughout)")
print(f"  Adadelta's accumulated sum: {adadelta_history[-1]:.4f} (stayed bounded)")
print(f"\nAdagrad's sum at step 50: {adagrad_history[49]:.4f}, at step 200: {adagrad_history[-1]:.4f}")
print(f"Adadelta's sum at step 50: {adadelta_history[49]:.4f}, at step 200: {adadelta_history[-1]:.4f}")

blocks.content: Running this example shows Adagrad's accumulated sum continuing to grow steadily across all 200 steps, while Adadelta's sum quickly stabilizes and stays bounded, directly confirming the sliding-window behavior covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Adadelta makes one deliberate change to fix Adagrad's ever-shrinking learning rate problem.
It uses a sliding, decaying window of recent squared gradients instead of unlimited accumulation.
A decay factor weights recent gradients more heavily, with old ones progressively fading out entirely.
This keeps the accumulated sum bounded, keeping learning rates usable throughout even long training runs.
It was originally designed to need no manually chosen learning rate at all, a genuinely distinctive property.
Real implementations often still include an optional learning rate parameter anyway, for practical flexibility.
Adagrad's sum grows without limit; Adadelta's stays bounded, directly solving that specific weakness.
RMSProp, covered next, was developed around the same time, addressing this same problem independently.
Next up: RMSProp, another closely related solution to the same ever-shrinking learning rate problem.
